geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better reconstructs the manometer as a filled, outlined U-tube with distinct glass walls, liquid regions, menisci, an open/closed right arm, pressure arrow, and height marker; Figure 1 captures the basic topology and pressure-level trend but uses thick centerline strokes rather than true filled tube geometry and, more importantly, leaves the closed-end cap line visible even in open-end mode, making the open arm structurally ambiguous. Figure 1 does include the three pressure cases clearly, but Figure 2’s apparatus proportions, fill/outline treatment, and open-versus-closed topology are more faithful overall.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2's controls update the liquid levels and active equation more consistently across the slider range, with the open-end plus/minus case determined by the actual gas pressure. Figure 1 covers more of the requested interaction list and has better formula-specific derivation popups, but its open-end radio buttons can become contradictory after moving the pressure slider, and selecting a mode changes the pressure value behind the user's back; its closed-end height is also capped at high pressures, so the displayed column no longer truly responds proportionally to P_gas.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 more closely matches the original closed-end manometer panel at a glance, with a similar left gas bulb, small valve, tall U-tube geometry, right closed tube, and labels placed like the textbook figure. Figure 2 is also recognizable, but the large circular valve/stopcock detail is an invented visual element that substantially changes the appearance, and its proportions/composition feel less like the original despite having a more complete formula label.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the key labels for the shown closed-end manometer more complete and readable, including a full bottom equation “P_gas = hρg,” clear “Gas,” “Closed end,” “Vacuum,” and “h” labels. Figure 1 includes most of these labels but its bottom formula is visibly incomplete, showing only “= hρg,” and it also has more cluttering instructional/control text, making its labeling less faithful and less clean.

concept.rationale: Both figures encode the core pressure relationships correctly in their normal states: closed-end vacuum gives P_gas = hρg, gas-side liquid higher in an open-end manometer gives P_gas = P_atm − hρg, and open-arm liquid higher gives P_gas = P_atm + hρg (L00014, L00017). Figure 2 is more conceptually accurate because it actually changes the right arm between an open top and a closed vacuum cap, while Figure 1 leaves a horizontal cap line visible even in open-end modes, visually contradicting the required open-to-atmosphere arm (L00010, L00014, L00017). Figure 1 also can display a selected radio label such as “gas below atm” while the pressure slider makes the geometry and equation switch to the above-atmosphere case, whereas Figure 2’s open-end state changes sign based on the gas pressure without keeping a contradictory case label (L00017).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger overall because it more accurately models the U-tube geometry, open-versus-closed arm state, liquid levels, pressure equations, and labels, while Figure 1 has structural ambiguity from leaving a cap line visible in open-end mode and can show contradictory open-end pressure states. Although Figure 1 more closely resembles the original screenshot composition and apparatus style, its incomplete formula label and less consistent interactivity make it weaker than Figure 2 on the higher-confidence conceptual, labeling, geometry, and interaction judgments.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the Hall-Héroult cell structure with a more complete enclosing shell/ceramic lining, crust, electrolyte, distinct molten aluminum layer, sloped carbon cathode floor, two immersed carbon anodes with forks/bus connection, negative/positive terminals, exhaust hood, and leader lines pointing to the correct regions. Figure 2 captures the main components but its layout is more schematic and compressed: the shell begins at the bath surface rather than visibly enclosing the cell, the electrolyte and molten aluminum boundaries/labels are less accurately placed, and the hood/anode support structure is much simplified, making the relative proportions and containment topology less faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1's controls coherently drive the advertised state: the play checkbox gates the reaction, the current slider increases bubble spawning and aluminum accumulation, and the step buttons synchronize the slider and play state. Figure 2's current slider does affect bubbles and pool thickness, but its run button is initially mislabeled/inverted, changing the slider can silently restart a paused animation, and it lacks the Al³⁺/O²⁻ ion animation that the interaction claims to show.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful overall: it preserves the original’s wide cross-section proportions, peach ceramic lining inside a dark steel shell, green electrolyte layer over gray molten aluminum, long black cathode, two anodes, white top bus bar with plus sign, and exhaust outline. Figure 2 is recognizable but more simplified and altered, with a more compact cell shape, a thick black top bus instead of the original outlined white bar, less accurate wall/lining geometry, and generally less resemblance to the original composition.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has substantially more readable diagram labels at inline size and includes the key original annotations such as Ceramic, Steel shell, Crust, bubbles, dissolved alumina/cryolite, molten aluminum, carbon anode/cathode, polarity signs, and HF exhaust. Figure 1 attempts most of the same labels but many are extremely small and cramped, especially the left-side material labels, anode labels, and right-side chemical annotations, making them much harder to read than Figure 2.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 teaches the chemistry more accurately: it identifies Al³⁺ reduction at the carbon cathode, oxide/anode gas formation, carbon anode consumption, the mixed O₂/CO/CO₂ bubbles, molten aluminum pooling on the cathode, and the cryolite temperature-lowering role in ways that align with the brief (L00012-L00014, L00019). Figure 1 has the main cell geometry and labels, but its anode tooltip misleadingly says “oxygen is oxidized to form CO and CO₂,” whereas the brief specifically frames the gases as forming at the anode as the carbon anodes are oxidized, and its process narration omits O₂ even though O₂ is one of the required anode products (L00007, L00012, L00019). Figure 2 is not perfect because its cathode is less clearly sloped than requested, but its core electrochemical assertions are more faithful overall (L00019).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall reconstruction because it more faithfully preserves the Hall-Héroult cell geometry and rendered appearance, with a more complete shell/lining structure, clearer containment layers, anodes, cathode, terminals, hood, and controls that behave coherently. Figure 2 has more readable labels and somewhat better chemical teaching details, but it is more schematic and compressed, with less accurate containment topology and weaker interaction behavior, including mislabeled/inverted run behavior and missing ion animation.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 is geometrically closer because it builds the intended convex loss surface over the correct-looking φ0/φ1 ranges, includes the floor and back grid panes, labeled axes and loss ticks, the specified example markers plus minimum/current marker, and a separate contour inset matching panel b. Figure 2 uses a different boxed coordinate frame and a different loss minimum/marker set, omits the simultaneous inset contour panel in favor of a view toggle/flattening animation, lacks the explicit minimum marker, and its proportions and loss scaling are less faithful to the original layout.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the intended interactive workflow more correctly: dragging the current parameter updates the surface marker, loss readout, and inset heatmap marker, and the learning-rate slider drives an animated descent with visibly different slow, stable, oscillatory, and divergent behavior. Figure 2’s controls mostly function, but it replaces the simultaneous surface/heatmap synchronization with a view toggle, its large-rate behavior is partly masked by clamping parameters to the domain, and its demo sequencing can change learning rate mid-run rather than restarting a clean overshoot example. Figure 1 has a minor edge-case flaw where a divergent final step can leave the 3D marker stale while the heatmap/readout update, but overall its handlers better recompute and redraw the advertised states.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more recognizable as the textbook figure because it shows both the 3D loss surface and the contour view with the same brown loss-color scheme, axis labels, and colored marker points, even though the panels overlap awkwardly and include some extra/wrong-colored points. Figure 2 has a cleaner single 3D view, but it omits the contour panel in the screenshot and its surface reads more like a generic bowl with added contour bands and darker styling, making the overall resemblance to the original multipanel figure weaker.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes most of the original figure's key labels across both the 3D surface and contour views, including panel marker a), axis labels for Intercept and Slope, and Loss labels, whereas Figure 2 only shows the 3D surface and therefore omits the contour-panel labels and the b) panel labeling entirely. Figure 1's labels are noticeably cluttered, small, and partly overlapping, especially around the transition between panels, but Figure 2 is worse overall because it is missing many required annotations and adds unrelated UI/demo text and an invented loss value label.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately teaches the intended relationship between the 3D supervised loss surface and its corresponding top-down heatmap: it shows both labeled panels a) and b) at once, uses the same convex quadratic loss and the same parameter markers in both views, and makes the global minimum visible in both representations as required (L00007). Figure 2’s quadratic surface is also conceptually convex and its parameter ranges and loss scaling are closer to the stated 0–70 vertical extent, but it replaces the two-panel comparison with a toggle/flattened single scene and does not clearly present panel labels or the simultaneous correspondence between the 3D surface and 2D contour heatmap, so a student would get a less faithful understanding of the figure’s intended two-view comparison (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear overall winner because it more faithfully recreates the intended two-panel figure: it shows both the 3D convex loss surface and the corresponding contour/heatmap view simultaneously, with the expected axes, panel labels, loss markings, and synchronized parameter markers. Figure 2 has a cleaner single-scene presentation and some functional controls, but it omits the simultaneous contour panel, lacks several required labels and markers, changes the coordinate framing and interaction model, and its large-learning-rate behavior is less faithful due to clamping and sequencing issues.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better reconstructs the figure as a 3D object: it uses a thin extruded photo slab, raised grid-strip geometry, layered tile planes, borders, token dots, and attention lines with an oblique camera that gives a clearer spatial structure. Figure 1 keeps almost everything as flat coplanar textured planes with only overlaid line segments and a low perspective view, so although its window counts and token subdivisions are useful, its geometry is much less three-dimensional and less physically faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 has the more reliable interactions overall: its slider, regular/offset buttons, step buttons, and tile-click overlay rebuild from the current state, and clicking a tile shows token dots plus all-pair attention lines confined to that current tile. Figure 1 handles the intended 1/2/4 and suppresses the degenerate 1×1 offset better, but its rebuilt tiles are never removed from the global interactive-object registry, so after changing the slider or offset toggle a click can hit stale, removed tiles from a previous partition and draw the wrong highlight/attention region; it also shows only a star from one token rather than clearly highlighting all tokens. Figure 2 is not perfect because its slider wrongly admits 3×3 and its 1×1 offset state draws extra partial windows despite the label, but its main click-and-redraw behavior is substantially more correct.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the oblique 3D wall-like composition and the dense window partitioning/gaps seen in the reference panels, so it reads more like the same windowed image decomposition. Figure 2 uses a much flatter front-facing square composition with a simplified invented cartoon/graffiti style and heavier black grid lines, making it look more like a generic tiled illustration than the perspective textbook figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has a clear caption under the rendered panel reading “4×4 windows,” which directly matches one of the original figure’s required labels, and its step labels also reference the original window cases. Figure 1 lacks the original-style panel caption under the artwork and instead relies on UI controls and a small explanatory paragraph, adding invented annotation text while omitting most of the textbook labels.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately preserves the requested partition cases: its 4×4, 2×2, offset variants, and degenerate 1×1 full-image window match the hierarchy and shifted-window idea in the brief, and it correctly prevents an offset from changing the 1×1 case (L00007). Figure 2 explains local window attention and alternating offset partitions well, but it can display a false “1×1 offset window” state that is actually split into multiple tiles, and its popup confusingly calls an individual tile a “4×4” or “2×2” window when those labels refer to the grid of windows, not the selected window itself (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger overall because it provides a clearer 3D reconstruction with raised/layered window geometry and more reliable interactive rebuilding, and it includes clearer original-style labels such as the “4×4 windows” caption. Figure 1 is visually closer in perspective and handles the 1×1/offset concept more correctly, but it is weaker geometrically, lacks the key panel-style labeling, and its stale interactive objects can cause clicks to highlight the wrong window after state changes.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the intended 3D geometry: it uses a true 3D joint box with slices perpendicular to the latent z direction, Gaussian blobs centered along a curved manifold, and a separate marginal x-space panel with the projected density. Figure 2 captures the general idea but permutes the geometry more awkwardly by making the slice planes move along world x while using the panel in a YZ plane, has a shallower/mismatched box, and its manifold/axis relationships are less faithful to the latent-z slicing structure of the source.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements all three intended interactions with mostly coherent handlers: the z slider moves the active slice and its blob/dot, the marginalization button sweeps z while progressively redrawing the marginal texture, and dragging the observation marker recomputes a posterior curve and MAP dot. Figure 2 only implements a z-slice slider; that handler does update the sweep plane and its density correctly, but it omits the marginalization animation and the draggable observation/posterior interaction entirely, so its interaction coverage and advertised VAE exploration are much weaker.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more recognizable as the textbook figure because it preserves the dominant visual structure of stacked dark brown probability slices in a 3D box, a prominent cyan trajectory with teal points, heatmap-like bright regions, and a marginal Pr(x|φ) panel. Figure 1 includes some correct elements, but the main cyan manifold is reduced to a small/awkward path, the 3D composition is much less like the reference, the marginal panel is tiny and misplaced, and extra UI/step controls visually dominate the screenshot.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has cleaner, more readable diagram labels with less clutter and far fewer invented annotations; Figure 1 includes many extra UI/button/instruction labels that are not in the original and distract from the figure. Figure 1 does include the marginal panel x1/x2 labels that Figure 2 appears to omit, but its overall label presentation is more crowded and mismatched to the textbook figure.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more truthfully represents the core VAE latent-variable relationship: its left panel uses constant-z slice planes carrying conditional density in the x1-x2 directions and a curved decoder manifold indexed by the scalar latent z, then constructs the right panel by summing/projecting those conditional blobs into an x1-x2 marginal, matching the intended joint-to-marginal story (L00007). Figure 2 also shows conditional slices and a marginal density, but it maps the latent variable to the world x direction while also labelling axes x1, x2, and z in a more confusing way, so a student is less clearly taught that z is the latent axis and x=(x1,x2) is the observed data plane (L00007). Both figures fall short of the brief’s multi-colored family of z-slice curves, but Figure 1 better preserves the mathematical relationship between Pr(x,z|phi), Pr(x|z,phi), and Pr(x|phi), and it more explicitly states the intractable/no-closed-form marginalization motivation than Figure 2 (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it more faithfully implements the intended latent-variable geometry and interactions: its z-aligned slices, curved decoder manifold, marginal x-space panel, z slider, marginalization sweep, and draggable observation/posterior behavior all support the VAE joint-to-marginal story. Figure 2 is visually cleaner and closer to the rendered textbook style, with better-looking stacked slices and less label clutter, but relative to Figure 1 it omits most intended interactions and uses a more confusing axis/slice arrangement that weakens the mathematical relationship between latent z, observed x, and the marginal density.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 at least constructs a coherent 3D pinhole-projection scene with an origin, image plane, birds along a 3D trajectory, rays, projected silhouettes, velocity arrows, and a vanishing point with consistent perspective formulas. Figure 2 is geometrically more ambitious in concept, but its source redeclares constants such as GTS, FOCAL, START, DIR, and helper vectors in the same module scope, causing a syntax error and preventing the figure from rendering at all, so it cannot accurately reconstruct the 3D geometry.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 at least loads and its time slider recomputes the bird positions, projections, projection rays, vanishing point, and image-plane velocity arrows, and its drag handle updates the flight direction components and redraws the dependent geometry, though it lacks the requested automatic looping animation and only allows a limited direction change. Figure 2 contains duplicate top-level const/let declarations such as FOCAL, START, DIR, GTS, tCur, and helper vectors, which causes a module syntax error before execution, so none of its advertised controls, animation, slider, demo buttons, or drag interaction can work.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 at least renders a recognizable miniature version of the intended perspective/vanishing-point scene with a framed plane, red motion arrows, small bird-like marks, and labels, whereas Figure 2 fails to render the visualization at all and only shows a JavaScript syntax error message.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 at least renders a diagram with some small annotations that appear to correspond to the original, although they are far too tiny and it adds an unrelated UI label, while Figure 2 fails to render the figure at all and only shows an error message and reload button instead of any required labels such as V, O, or Vanishing point.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 renders a coherent pinhole-camera construction: a constant straight 3D translation with equal red V arrows projects through O onto an image plane, with image-plane arrows computed from successive projections so they shrink toward the vanishing point, matching the core concepts in the brief (L00008-L00013, L00016). Figure 2 would conceptually include more of the requested image-plane/inset explanation, but its source redeclares constants such as GTS, FOCAL, START, DIR, tCur, and helper vectors in the same module scope, causing a JavaScript syntax error before rendering; as a result it cannot actually teach the stated convergence/vanishing-point relationships (L00013-L00016).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear winner because it renders a coherent pinhole-projection scene with birds, rays, image plane, velocity arrows, labels, vanishing point, and working time/direction controls. Figure 2 may have aimed for a richer explanation, but duplicate top-level declarations cause a JavaScript syntax error, so it fails to render and none of its labels, geometry, or interactions are available.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately reconstructs the intended 3D camera-projection geometry: it includes a real 3D house with roof, windows, depth, a point P on the object face, correctly placed virtual and sensor planes at ±f, a sensor grid with M/N proportions, ray intersections, brackets, axes, and a pixelated sensor image. Figure 2 captures the broad pinhole-camera idea but replaces the object with a mostly flat decorative panel, places P disconnected from that panel, uses less faithful proportions and simplified ranges, and omits the richer projected-object/pixel sampling geometry that Figure 1 models.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1’s main controls consistently recompute and redraw the projection, grid, snapped pixel, and readout: dragging P updates both projections, sliders update geometry and sampling, radio readout modes report the intended quantities, and its demo-step buttons actually synchronize slider values and state. Figure 2 has some stronger requested readouts such as pixel size and K, but its “Sensor-centered” mode computes offset corner-based coordinates rather than centered sensor coordinates, its pixel index convention is less consistent with the intended top-left image indexing, and its demo-step buttons are effectively broken because the tween is assigned before the `if (!tween)` check, so most advertised step changes never run or redraw.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more recognizable as the textbook diagram because it preserves the key structure of a camera projection setup: a colored scene/object, point P, optical axis, camera center, virtual image plane, and gridded sensor plane with coordinate labels. Figure 1 includes a sensor grid and projection line, but its scene is reduced to a house-like block and the overall arrangement omits or minimizes many of the distinctive axes, labels, and layered planes that make the original identifiable.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 includes many more of the original diagram annotations in the rendered scene, such as P, optical/principal axis, Zc/Yc, camera center, virtual image plane, image plane/sensor, N pixels, M pixels, and f, whereas Figure 1’s scene labels are mostly absent or too tiny to read and relies mainly on unrelated UI/control text. Figure 2’s labels are still small, but they better match the required textbook labels and are placed around the corresponding objects more clearly than Figure 1.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 represents the core geometry more consistently: a ray from P passes through the pinhole at the camera-coordinate origin to a virtual plane at +f and an inverted physical sensor at −f, then is quantized to a pixel cell on an N-by-M grid, matching the requested image-formation and sampling chain (L00012, L00015). Figure 2 also shows these elements, but its displayed intrinsic matrix uses positive fx, fy while its actual sensor pixel indices are computed from the inverted behind-the-pinhole coordinates sx = −fX/Z, sy = −fY/Z, so the K it asserts would not map to the pixel indices it displays; it also labels offset physical coordinates as “sensor-centered,” which is conceptually misleading for the principal-point-offset discussion (L00009-L00012, L00015).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it more consistently implements the intended pinhole-camera geometry: a 3D object point projects through the camera center to virtual and sensor planes, updates correctly under controls, and quantizes onto a pixel grid. Figure 2 is more visually recognizable and better labeled in the rendered screenshot, but relative to Figure 1 it has less faithful source geometry, inconsistent sensor-centered/index computations, and broken demo-step behavior, so its stronger annotations do not outweigh the underlying geometric and conceptual issues.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately reconstructs the full 3D calibration/reprojection geometry: it has a correctly scaled image plane at the focal distance, three world points and corresponding projected/reprojected image points, filled triangles in both 3D and on the image plane, split projection rays, and true 3D residual cylinders with coherent camera-pose controls. Figure 2 captures the broad idea but uses a flipped coordinate setup and behind-view workaround, a disproportionately large shifted image plane, simpler single dashed rays and flat line error vectors, and omits some spatial elements such as the full mini image-plane tripod, making its geometry less faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 covers and mostly wires the intended interactions: its focal length, yaw, and translation sliders recompute all reprojected points and residual/SSE displays, and its aggregate toggle correctly switches between per-point numeric residuals and total SSE. Figure 2's focal and translation sliders and SSE toggle work, but it has no dragging of observed or reprojected points at all, no rotation/pose slider beyond translation, and no per-point numeric residual display. Figure 1 is not flawless—the dragged reprojected point is not integrated into updateAll, its label/SSE can go stale, and dragging observed points mutates world points while leaving the world triangle geometry stale—but these are still less limiting than Figure 2 omitting major requested controls entirely.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because it preserves the original’s overall composition: a large orange 3D triangle on the right, a projection plane on the left with a smaller projected orange triangle, colored vertices, dashed correspondence lines, and green coordinate axes. Figure 1 includes some of the same ingredients, but the projection plane is positioned awkwardly behind/right of the main triangle, the projected triangle is very small and hard to read, and the overall layout is much less recognizable as the textbook figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the better label quality because its main diagram is larger and the point labels such as P1, P2, P3 and several projected p labels are more readable and better placed. Figure 1 shrinks the actual figure so much that most textbook-relevant labels are tiny or unreadable, with many original annotations effectively lost; both figures include extraneous UI/control text not present in the original, but Figure 2 preserves the diagram labels more successfully.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately teaches the full stated setup: it shows observed image points and reprojected points from the same 3D triangle, with red residual segments on the image plane and an objective explicitly written as Σ||pᵢ−p′ᵢ||², matching the definition of reprojection error as the 2D distance between observed and estimated projections (L00013-L00025, L00028). Figure 2 also represents the main residual idea, but it is less conceptually faithful because its controls reduce the estimated camera model mostly to focal length and an ambiguously labelled “Camera Pos X (T),” whereas the context describes estimated K, R, and T parameters; Figure 1 represents K, R, and T more directly (L00017-L00021).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it more accurately implements the 3D reprojection setup, including coherent camera pose/focal controls, observed versus reprojected image points, residuals, and the SSE objective, whereas Figure 2 simplifies the geometry with a shifted/flipped setup and lacks several key interactions such as rotation and point dragging. Figure 2 is more visually recognizable and has more readable labels, but those screenshot-level strengths do not outweigh its weaker reconstruction of the intended calibration/reprojection mechanics compared with Figure 1.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the core 2D translation structure: the original, translated, and final squares are connected by straight solid red vectors t, s, and the resultant t+s with arrowheads, matching the expected vector-addition geometry. Figure 2 includes the same basic nodes but makes the t+s resultant a curved arrow, which is structurally less accurate for a translation vector, and it adds extra dashed drag rings that are not part of the underlying textbook diagram.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 has more complete and generally correct interaction paths: dragging the arrow handles or squares and using the tx/ty/sx/sy sliders all redraw the geometry and update the displayed homogeneous and composed matrices. Figure 1’s basic drag and chain toggle work, but it offers fewer direct controls and has weaker degenerate handling, e.g. zero-length vectors leave labels at stale positions because label placement returns without updating. Figure 2 is not perfect—its s sliders can be clamped/reset when the requested final point would leave the allowed domain, and manually toggling chain mode can leave the step narration out of sync—but overall its controls recompute and display the intended translation composition more completely than Figure 1.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is much more visually faithful: it preserves the large black arrowed axes, serif axis labels, orange squares with thick black outlines, and the red translation arrow labeled t in a composition that closely resembles the left panel of the reference. Figure 1 has the same basic elements but renders them much smaller with thin gray axes, a light grid, different proportions, and extra matrix/UI clutter that make it look less like the original textbook figure at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the required diagram labels x, y, and t in large, readable type placed close to the corresponding axes/vector, whereas Figure 1’s x, y, and t labels are much smaller and less comfortable to read at inline size. Both figures add extra interface/instructional text not present in the textbook, but Figure 1’s extra matrix and control labels are more visually prominent relative to its small diagram labels, making the original annotations less effective.

concept.rationale: Both figures correctly show a translation as adding a vector to the square’s position and correctly show two translations composing to the vector sum t+s (L00007-L00023, L00026, L00053-L00054). Figure 2 is conceptually stronger because it explicitly states the coordinate update (x, y, 1) → (x+tx, y+ty, 1) and the matrix composition T(s)·T(t)=T(t+s), directly matching the homogeneous-coordinate motivation (L00028-L00030, L00053-L00054), whereas Figure 1’s geometry is mostly correct but its matrix composition is less explicit, presenting adjacent matrices without a clear multiplication symbol and relying more on narration.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger overall because it much more closely matches the rendered textbook-style diagram, with prominent black axes, readable x/y/t labels, orange outlined squares, and it provides more complete interactive controls with matrix and coordinate updates. Compared with Figure 2, Figure 1 has more accurate straight-vector geometry for the resultant t+s, but its diagram is visually smaller and cluttered by UI/matrix text, its labels are less readable, and its interaction handling is less complete. Figure 2’s curved resultant arrow and extra drag rings are weaknesses relative to Figure 1, but they are outweighed by its higher faithfulness, clearer labeling, and stronger conceptual/interactivity coverage.
